section_summary: This section documents State and Commerce Department efforts to monitor and enforce the voluntary “moral embargo” on aviation fuel technology, aircraft equipment, strategic materials, and other exports to Japan, alongside statistical reports on trade with Japan, the Soviet Union, and Mexico. It includes exchanges with Petro-Chem Development Company and United States Gauge Company, as well as internal concern that Japanese trading companies could evade the policy by buying goods through American intermediaries. A substantial portion records public and congressional pressure for statutory embargoes on war materials, petroleum, and scrap exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Memorandum concerning possible violations of the aviation-gasoline moral embargo
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Reports information from F. E. Johnson Jr. about individuals allegedly supplying aviation-gasoline production information to Japanese and Soviet interests.
subfiles.summary: Johnson alleged that Swanson, Wallie, and Throckmorton, formerly of the dissolved Alco Company, had formed a New York firm that might be supplying technical information to Asano Busan. He also less confidently identified industrial chemist Clarence P. Harrie as possibly supplying similar information to Amtorg, and Yost promised to bring the moral-embargo policy to their attention.

subfiles.title: Letter to Petro-Chem Development Company concerning aviation-gasoline information
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Requests disclosure of any negotiations involving aviation-gasoline technology and an assurance of cooperation with the moral embargo.
subfiles.summary: Yost recalls the Department's February 28 letter enclosing its December 20, 1939 policy statement on high-quality aviation gasoline. Petro-Chem is asked whether it has negotiated with representatives of countries engaged in bombing civilians and whether the Department may expect its future cooperation.

subfiles.title: Counselor's memorandum on the Pittman Japanese Resolution
subfiles.from: The Counselor of the Department of State
subfiles.about: Discusses consulting Senator Pittman about the prospects for and desired timing of his Japanese resolution.
subfiles.summary: The Counselor proposes that he and Hackworth meet Pittman to learn whether the resolution would pass if brought forward. Pittman had previously said that he was awaiting a signal from the Department and might hesitate unless the Secretary unequivocally favored action.

subfiles.title: Confidential transmittal of April moral-embargo export statistics
subfiles.from: Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce
subfiles.about: Transmits a confidential statistical report on April shipments of commodities associated with the moral embargo.
subfiles.summary: The report covers declarations received through April 22 and is supplied for information rather than dissemination. Mexico is included despite not being subject to the moral embargo because of the possibility of transshipment trade.

subfiles.title: Exports of commodities subject to the moral embargo through April 22
subfiles.from: Division of Foreign Trade Statistics, Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce
subfiles.about: Lists quantities and values of selected April exports to Japan, the Soviet Union, and Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The table records Japanese imports of scrap rubber and substantial aircraft parts and accessories, Soviet imports of tin slabs, and a broad range of Mexican rubber, silk, metal, and aviation products. A note emphasizes that Mexico was not itself subject to the moral embargo.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on ineffective enforcement of the aircraft moral embargo
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Evaluates investigations of large aircraft-product exports to Japan and recommends stronger access to exporter information.
subfiles.summary: Yost reports that Commerce officials investigated major January and April aircraft shipments but obtained little cooperation from an American manufacturer, which described the goods as replacement parts for commercial planes. Other shipments were made by agents acting for Japanese firms such as Mitsui and Mitsubishi, and Commerce officials considered approaches to those firms futile. Yost argues that Commerce's administration of the moral embargo has failed and suggests obtaining exporter names and requiring declarations to identify the American manufacturers supplying Japanese interests.

subfiles.title: Analysis of petroleum-product exports to Japan and the Soviet Union
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes changes in aviation gasoline, regular gasoline, crude petroleum, and lubricating-oil exports.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum finds that exports of all four petroleum categories to Japan declined during the first quarter of 1940, although their aggregate value remained significant. Petroleum exports to the Soviet Union were far smaller and generally declining or negligible.

subfiles.title: Preliminary petroleum-export statistics for the first quarter of 1940
subfiles.from: Harold W. Moseley, Department of State
subfiles.about: Provides monthly values and barrel quantities for petroleum exports to Japan and the Soviet Union, with annual comparisons for 1938 and 1939.
subfiles.summary: The tables compare January through March 1940 exports of aviation gasoline, regular gasoline, crude petroleum, and lubricating oils with full-year totals for 1938 and 1939. They show substantial shipments to Japan but almost no aviation gasoline or crude petroleum going to the Soviet Union.

subfiles.title: Petro-Chem assurance of compliance with the moral embargo
subfiles.from: H. R. Swanson, President, Petro-Chem Development Company
subfiles.to: Department of State, attention Charles W. Yost
subfiles.about: Denies conducting prohibited negotiations and promises cooperation with the Department's aviation-gasoline policy.
subfiles.summary: Swanson states that since the policy announcement Petro-Chem has not negotiated with representatives of countries bombing or machine-gunning civilians. He expressly promises the company's cooperation in withholding plans, plants, manufacturing rights, and technical information for high-quality aviation gasoline.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Petro-Chem's cooperation
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Petro-Chem's denial of restricted negotiations and its promise to cooperate.
subfiles.summary: The Department restates the assurances contained in Petro-Chem's May 21 letter. It notes with gratification the company's promised cooperation with the policy on aviation-gasoline technology.

subfiles.title: Senator Ashurst's transmittal of Dr. Watson's inquiry
subfiles.from: Henry F. Ashurst
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's inquiry about trade with Japan and requests information for a reply.
subfiles.summary: Ashurst sends Hull a letter from Dr. Samuel H. Watson of Tucson. He asks the Department to investigate Watson's inquiry, advise him of the result, and return the enclosure.

subfiles.title: Dr. Watson's appeal for an embargo on war materials to Japan
subfiles.from: Samuel H. Watson
subfiles.about: Asks whether American exports are enabling Japanese aggression and urges a statutory embargo if so.
subfiles.summary: Watson asks Ashurst to determine whether the United States is selling Japan materials that strengthen it as a potential military opponent and facilitate the destruction of China. He urges Congress to embargo war materials destined for Japan if that understanding is correct.

subfiles.title: Secretary Hull's reply to Senator Ashurst on trade with Japan
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Supplies a standard Department response explaining existing policy and sources of trade statistics.
subfiles.summary: Hull explains that no statute authorizes the comprehensive embargo Watson advocates, but cites presidential policies discouraging aircraft, aeronautical materials, and aviation-gasoline technology exports to countries bombing civilians. He notes that the few 1940 munitions export licenses for Japan concerned contracts predating the policy and directs Ashurst to National Munitions Control Board and Commerce Department publications. Watson's letter is returned with reports and a press release.

subfiles.title: United States Gauge Company inquiry about Japanese aircraft-instrument sales
subfiles.from: R. N. Gierse, United States Gauge Company
subfiles.about: Requests guidance after a Japanese Army officer sought company catalogues for aircraft-related gauges.
subfiles.summary: The company quotes an April 26 request from Flight Lieutenant Colonel Haruo Odagiri of the Japanese Army's Aero-Experimental Department for all catalogues issued since 1939. It asks whether any current rule governs sales of airplane instruments by American vendors to the Japanese government.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to United States Gauge Company
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the moral-embargo policy applicable to possible sales of aircraft instruments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges the company's inquiry concerning the Japanese Army's Aero-Experimental Department. He encloses the President's December 2, 1939 statement and the Department's December 15 release and explains that the policy covers aeronautical equipment and materials essential to aircraft manufacture.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference concerning aviation-gasoline production data
subfiles.from: Department of State records staff
subfiles.about: Points to a confidential telegram from France concerning unauthorized transfer of aviation-gasoline technology to the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: The note records Frank A. Howard's report that German authorities had sold unspecified Standard Oil Development Company production data to the Soviet Union without company permission. It adds that the company would not sell such information to Japan and directs the reader to Bullitt's telegram number 608 in another file.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Senator Maloney's requests about war-material shipments
subfiles.from: C. W. Barnes, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Records assistance given to Senator Maloney in answering protests against shipments of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Maloney's office requested explanatory material and, in one constituent case, the names of exporting companies. Barnes sent National Munitions Control Board and press-release materials on May 24 and advised the senator's office that no statute authorized an embargo on war-material sales to Japan.

subfiles.title: Duplicate memorandum on Senator Maloney's requests
subfiles.from: C. W. Barnes, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Duplicates the memorandum describing the Department's response to Senator Maloney's inquiry.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats that Maloney sought material for answering constituent protests and a request for exporter names. It records the publications sent and the Department's statement that existing law did not authorize an embargo on war-material sales to Japan.

subfiles.title: Senator Byrd's transmittal of H. P. Johnson's telegram
subfiles.from: Harry F. Byrd
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent telegram questioning trade in munitions materials with Japan and requests comment.
subfiles.summary: Byrd encloses a telegram from H. P. Johnson of Charlottesville. He asks Hull to provide the Department's comments on Johnson's questions.

subfiles.title: Telegram questioning continued munitions trade with Japan
subfiles.from: H. P. Johnson
subfiles.about: Questions why the United States continues selling Japan materials used to make munitions.
subfiles.summary: Johnson asks whether American firms are still supplying Japan with the ingredients of munitions. He also asks whether those same firms supply the United States and whether their interests explain why trade cannot be stopped.

subfiles.title: Secretary Hull's reply to Senator Byrd
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Acknowledges H. P. Johnson's telegram and introduces the Department's customary response to such trade complaints.
subfiles.summary: Hull thanks Byrd for forwarding Johnson's telegram concerning trade with Japan. The surviving text says that the Department normally answers similar communications with a standard paragraph, but that paragraph is not reproduced on the page.

subfiles.title: Additional duplicate memorandum on Senator Maloney's requests
subfiles.from: C. W. Barnes, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Provides another duplicate of the record concerning assistance to Senator Maloney.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum again describes requests for material on war-material shipments to Japan, including the names of exporting companies. It records the reports and press releases furnished and the explanation that no existing statute authorized an embargo.

subfiles.title: Representative Hope's request for the government's position on exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Clifford R. Hope
subfiles.about: Requests a public explanation of government policy for use in answering constituents concerned about exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hope encloses a letter representative of many he has received on the subject. He asks Hull to outline the government's position as fully as it can then be made public so that he can provide a reasonable response.

subfiles.title: Harry Faris's appeal to stop strategic exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Harry Faris, Cornell & Company
subfiles.about: Argues that exports of fuel, scrap, ammunition, and other supplies are helping Japan wage war in China.
subfiles.summary: Faris supports adequate national defense but compares American trade with Japan to earlier British assistance that helped Hitler build Germany's military power. He contends that American gasoline, oil, scrap iron, ammunition, and other supplies sustain Japan's war in China and asks Congress to end that assistance.

subfiles.title: Secretary Hull's initial reply to Representative Hope
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Provides the Department's standard legal response to Harry Faris's demand for an embargo.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Hope's letter and the enclosed communication from Harry Faris. He states that no current statute authorizes the proposed embargo and that new legislation would be required before one could be imposed, then returns the enclosure.

subfiles.title: Representative Hope's follow-up question on embargo legislation
subfiles.from: Clifford R. Hope
subfiles.about: Asks whether any substantive reason exists not to enact legislation authorizing an embargo on war materials for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hope says Hull's May 27 legal explanation does not answer his underlying concern. He asks the Department to explain whether there is any good reason Congress should refrain from authorizing an embargo.

subfiles.title: Secretary Hull's reply on the policy implications of an embargo
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Declines to reduce the embargo question to a simple written answer and offers an in-person policy discussion.
subfiles.summary: Hull explains that Hope's question requires careful weighing of both short-term and long-term consequences and cannot be covered adequately in a letter. He offers to discuss the matter personally or have a knowledgeable associate meet Hope at the Department or his office.

subfiles.title: Chairman Sabath's appeal for action on scrap-export resolutions
subfiles.from: Adolph J. Sabath, House Committee on Rules
subfiles.about: Urges consideration of pending resolutions to embargo scrap-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Sabath reports that his committee has several embargo resolutions before it and has received thousands of increasingly numerous letters supporting action. He argues that restricting scrap exports would have nationwide approval and could be justified by the United States' own immediate defense requirements.

subfiles.title: Secretary Hull's reply concerning authority to restrict scrap exports
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Points to pending national-defense legislation as a more workable means of restricting scrap-material exports.
subfiles.summary: Hull agrees that domestic defense requirements for scrap are important and cites an amendment to H.R. 9850 authorizing restrictions and penalties. He notes that an identical provision was before the Senate and argues that enactment would let the President restrict scrap exports for national defense while avoiding the administrative problems posed by separate embargo resolutions.

subfiles.title: Commerce memorandum transmitting later April moral-embargo statistics
subfiles.from: Bernard Barton, Division of Foreign Trade Statistics
subfiles.about: Transmits a confidential report on additional April export declarations received through May 6.
subfiles.summary: Barton sends statistics covering declarations received from April 23 through May 6 for commodities associated with the moral embargo. He marks the material confidential and not for dissemination.

subfiles.title: Exports of commodities subject to the moral embargo through May 6
subfiles.from: Division of Foreign Trade Statistics, Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce
subfiles.about: Lists selected exports to Mexico and Japan reported in late-filed April declarations.
subfiles.summary: The report records Mexican shipments of rubber, silk, ferroalloys, aluminum, tin goods, aircraft, engines, instruments, and parts. Japanese shipments include scrap rubber, antimony regulus, wolfram ore, quicksilver, molybdenum concentrates, and several categories of aircraft parts and instruments, with notes explaining delayed declarations.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese-company exports of wolfram and quicksilver
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Investigates strategic-material shipments assembled and exported by Japanese companies operating in the United States.
subfiles.summary: Yost asked Barton about shipments of 194,987 pounds of wolfram ore and 7,003 pounds of quicksilver to Japan, while noting that scrap rubber was outside the moral embargo. Barton reported that Japanese companies in the United States had exported both commodities, apparently after assembling small open-market purchases in New York. Yost concludes that no effective means had been found to control such transactions and suggests consulting Treasury and Commerce about stricter enforcement if they continued; the final page carries a brief May 27 handwritten filing or routing comment.
